What Is a Buying Committee?

Explainerlowob research

By lowob · 13 November 2026 · 5-minute read · Revenue

A buying committee is the group of people at a customer organisation who take part in deciding a business-to-business purchase: those who use, evaluate, fund, approve and contract for it. Researchers call it the buying centre; Gartner and Forrester call it the buying group. Recent surveys put it at 5 to 16 people, and conflict within it is common.

What a buying committee means

Few B2B purchases are made by one person. A software tool is used by one team, assessed by IT, paid from another budget, reviewed by legal and approved by an executive. Any of them can stop it.

The concept comes from organisational buying research. Frederick Webster and Yoram Wind's 1972 paper in the Journal of Marketing modelled industrial buying as "an organizational decision-making process". It set out a concept of roles within the buying centre that later researchers extended. In 1982 Wind and Robertson proposed a sixth, "pin" role to manage interaction inside and outside the group. Wesley Johnston and Thomas Bonoma's 1981 study in the same journal measured real buying centres across 31 firms and 62 purchases, using 241 interviews.

"Buying centre" is the academic term, "buying group" the analysts' and "buying committee" the sellers'. They describe the same thing, though a formal committee is only one form it takes.

How large it is

SourceYearFindingSample
Johnston and Bonoma, Journal of Marketing1981Size grows with purchase importance, complexity and formalisation; services involve fewer people than capital equipment31 firms, 62 purchases
Gartner, buyer enablement researchUndatedTypical group of six to ten stakeholdersMore than 250 B2B customers
Forrester, State of Business Buying202413 people on average; 89% of purchases involve two or more departmentsNot stated in the release
Gartner, sales survey20255 to 16 people across up to four functions632 B2B buyers

Samples and definitions differ, but the direction is consistent: more people than a seller usually meets, from more than one department.

Why it matters for a commercial team

Consensus is the hard part. Gartner's May 2025 release defines unhealthy conflict as members having "conflicting objectives", disagreeing on the best course of action, or being overruled by external decision-makers. It found that content tailored to the group's shared needs improved consensus by 20%, while content focused only on individual relevance reduced it by 59%. Messaging each person separately can pull the group apart, which is the argument of Positioning for Complex Markets: give each role a reason to agree to one position.

Single-threaded deals are fragile. A deal with one engaged contact depends on that person's influence and tenure. Revenue intelligence tools flag it as a risk.

Scoring should follow the group. The case for scoring accounts rather than individual leads is set out in Lead Scoring vs Account Scoring.

In lowob's model the committee is data in the store, attached to the opportunity as contact roles. Who approved, who objected hardest and who was never reached also feed win-loss reviews and the deal's decision record.

How to map a buying committee

An illustrative role map for a mid-size services purchase. Role names vary by framework; MEDDICC, for example, names an economic buyer and a champion.

RoleWhat they care aboutWhat to record in the CRMWarning sign
Economic buyerReturn and risk to the budgetName, confirmed budget, decision dateNever met by the seller
ChampionSolving the problem they ownName, the case they will make internallyChampion cannot name the approver
User leadDaily workload and fitName, requirements raisedNo user has seen the solution
Technical or IT reviewerSecurity, integration, dataName, review statusReview not started inside the quarter
ProcurementTerms, price, supplier riskName, process and timelineProcess discovered at the last minute
LegalLiability and contract termsName, redline statusRedlines arrive after the close date

Ask early who else will be involved, and record every answer as a contact role. Build a mutual action plan with a named buyer owner for each step. At each pipeline meeting, check which roles are empty on late-stage deals. Agents can draft role-specific follow-ups, but each goes to the account owner before sending, because a message to the wrong member can undo a champion's work.

lowob takeaways

  • Assume a group. Most B2B purchases involve people from more than one department.
  • Sell to agreement. Consensus predicts deal quality better than any one person's enthusiasm.
  • Record roles on the opportunity. Empty roles on late-stage deals are a forecast risk.
  • Score the account, not the lead. One contact's activity says little about the committee.

Common questions

Who is on a B2B buying committee?

Typically an economic buyer, a champion, users, technical reviewers, procurement and legal. The mix depends on the purchase.

How many people are on a buying committee?

Forrester's 2024 research found 13 on average. Gartner's 2025 survey found 5 to 16 people across up to four functions.

What is the difference between a buying committee and a buying centre?

None in substance. Buying centre is the academic term from organisational buying research; buying committee and buying group are the sales and analyst terms.

Sources and notes

  • Johnston and Bonoma, The Buying Center: Structure and Interaction Patterns, Journal of Marketing Vol. 45, No. 3, Summer 1981. Academic study; university-hosted copy; small sample of 31 firms.
  • Webster and Wind, A General Model for Understanding Organizational Buying Behavior, Journal of Marketing Vol. 36, No. 2, April 1972. Bibliographic record and abstract only; full text behind a paywall.
  • Kemmerling and Herbst, A Status Quo of Buying Center Analysis, IMP Group conference paper, undated, references to 2013. Academic literature review; source for the Wind and Robertson pin role.
  • Forrester, To Master B2B Buying Mayhem, Providers Must Prioritize Buyers' Needs, 4 December 2024. Analyst press release; sample size for this study not stated.
  • Gartner, Sales Survey Finds 74% of B2B Buyer Teams Demonstrate "Unhealthy Conflict", 7 May 2025. Analyst press release; 632 buyers surveyed August to September 2024.
  • Gartner, Buyer Enablement, undated. Analyst research summary; survey date not given.
